question: A client asks: 'Why does LiveKit use an SFU instead of peer-to-peer WebRTC for voice agents?' What is the correct explanation?
options: An SFU (Selective Forwarding Unit) routes media server-side, so participants only send one upstream and receive one downstream per track. This scales better than P2P's N×N mesh, enables server-side features like recording and transcription, and lets agents participate as server-side endpoints without browser limitations.

P2P WebRTC requires each participant to maintain a direct connection to every other participant, which works for two-party calls but breaks down at scale. The SFU solves this by transcoding all media into a universal format server-side, reducing bandwidth requirements by 80% and enabling features like server-side recording through the transcoding pipeline.

P2P connections rely on STUN/TURN for NAT traversal, which adds 200-500ms of latency per hop. An SFU eliminates NAT traversal entirely by acting as a public relay endpoint, giving every participant a direct low-latency path. This is why LiveKit achieves sub-50ms media delivery even across continents.

P2P WebRTC was designed for browser-to-browser communication and has no mechanism for server-side processes to join as participants. LiveKit's SFU extends the WebRTC spec with a custom signaling protocol that allows headless agent processes to publish and subscribe to tracks using server-side WebRTC libraries.
explanation: The SFU model means each participant sends media once to the server, and the server forwards it to all subscribers. This avoids the N×N bandwidth explosion of P2P mesh topologies. It also enables server-side processing (recording, transcription, AI agent participation) that P2P cannot support. The SFU does not transcode — it selectively forwards packets.

question: In a LiveKit room with a voice agent, how many participants are present and what are their roles?
options: Two participants — a STANDARD participant (the browser user who publishes microphone audio) and an AGENT participant (the server-side agent that publishes TTS audio). Both connect to the same room, publish tracks, and subscribe to each other's tracks through the SFU.

Three participants — a STANDARD participant (the user), an AGENT participant (the AI logic), and a MEDIA participant (the SFU bridge that handles audio routing between them). The MEDIA participant is invisible to application code but handles codec negotiation and track forwarding.

Two participants — both are STANDARD type, but the agent's token includes an 'agent' grant that unlocks server-side capabilities like tool calling and TTS publishing. The participant type is the same; the token grants determine behavior.

Two participants — a STANDARD participant and an AGENT participant. The key difference is that the AGENT participant connects via a persistent gRPC stream rather than WebRTC, which gives it lower latency and access to server-side APIs that WebRTC participants cannot use.
explanation: A voice AI session has two participants in one room. The browser user is a STANDARD participant publishing microphone audio. The agent is an AGENT participant publishing TTS audio. The SFU routes media between them. There is no special 'agent mode' — the architecture is the same as any LiveKit application. Both use WebRTC.

question: What happens when a participant publishes a track in a LiveKit room where auto-subscribe is enabled?
options: The SFU detects the new track publication and begins transcoding it into each subscriber's preferred codec format. Once transcoding is ready, it pushes the transcoded stream to all participants. This ensures codec compatibility but adds 50-100ms of processing latency.

The SFU notifies all other participants via the signaling channel, and each client's SDK automatically sends a subscribe request back to the SFU. The SFU then begins forwarding media packets to each subscriber. This two-step handshake ensures reliable delivery.

The SFU notifies all other participants, which automatically begin receiving the track's media packets — no manual subscription needed. The SFU performs selective forwarding, routing packets without transcoding.

The track is buffered server-side for 500ms to accumulate enough data for smooth playback, then the SFU begins streaming to all subscribers simultaneously. This buffering ensures all participants receive the track at the same time, preventing sync issues.
explanation: With auto-subscribe (the default), when a new track is published, the SFU automatically forwards it to all other participants. The SFU does selective forwarding — it routes packets without transcoding. This is why agent audio reaches the browser immediately after the agent starts speaking.

question: A client is concerned about audio quality. They ask about LiveKit's codec strategy. What is the correct answer?
options: LiveKit's SFU performs selective forwarding — it routes media packets without transcoding. Participants negotiate codecs during WebRTC connection setup. Opus is the standard codec for voice, offering excellent quality at low bitrates with built-in packet loss concealment.

LiveKit's SFU negotiates the optimal codec between all participants during room setup. If participants support different codecs, the SFU transcodes in real-time to bridge the gap. Opus is preferred, but the SFU can transcode between Opus, G.711, and AAC transparently to maximize compatibility.

LiveKit enforces Opus as the mandatory codec for all audio tracks. During WebRTC negotiation, the SFU rejects any SDP offer that does not include Opus. This standardization eliminates codec mismatch issues and ensures consistent quality, since Opus provides excellent quality at 24-48 kbps with built-in FEC.

LiveKit uses adaptive codec selection — the SFU monitors network conditions and dynamically switches between Opus (high quality, higher bandwidth) and G.711 (lower quality, more resilient) based on packet loss rates. This happens transparently without interrupting the audio stream.
explanation: The SFU forwards packets without transcoding — this is the 'selective forwarding' part. Codec negotiation happens during WebRTC signaling. Opus is the standard for voice, providing high quality at low bitrates (typically 24-48 kbps for speech) with built-in forward error correction. The SFU does not transcode or dynamically switch codecs.

question: How are rooms created and destroyed in LiveKit?
options: Rooms are created on demand when the first participant joins a room name, and automatically cleaned up when all participants disconnect. The room name is specified in the JWT token grant.

Rooms must be created via the server-side API (CreateRoom) before any participant can join. This ensures room configuration (max participants, codec settings, recording options) is set before the first connection. Rooms are destroyed automatically after a configurable idle timeout, defaulting to 5 minutes.

Rooms are created on demand when the first participant joins. However, rooms persist for 30 minutes after the last participant disconnects to allow reconnection. This grace period is configurable via the room's empty_timeout setting. After the timeout, the room and all its metadata are permanently deleted.

Rooms are created via dispatch rules that map incoming connection requests to room names. The dispatch system determines room creation policy — whether to create a new room per session or reuse existing rooms. Rooms are destroyed when the dispatch rule's TTL expires, regardless of participant count.
explanation: LiveKit rooms are ephemeral by default. Joining a room name that doesn't exist creates it. When the last participant leaves, the room is cleaned up. This model maps perfectly to voice AI — each conversation gets its own room (often named with a UUID or session ID), keeping conversations isolated.
